items.title: ‘Some things you just don’t take off the menu’: Denny’s stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback
items.summary:
When Jensen Huang lost his job as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, he also lost his commemorative plaque at Denny’s. Eleven days later, Huang returned to the helm of the chip giant to a rock-star welcome from cheering employees. His plaque, it turns out, beat him to the comeback.

Now the restaurant chain has a message for its most famous former dishwasher. “Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” Denny’s wrote in a statement on social media on Wednesday.

Long before Huang became one of the most powerful people in the artificial intelligence industry, he was washing dishes at Denny’s. Years later, he and two friends met at one of the chain’s restaurants in San Jose, Calif., to discuss an idea that would become Nvidia, now ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the list’s most valuable company when the ranking was published in June.

On Sept. 26, 2023, Denny’s unveiled a plaque commemorating that very spot, calling it “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company.”

Denny’s defends its former employee 

The plaque came down on the evening of Nov. 12, an employee at the San Jose restaurant told SFGATE . That was the same day Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China. Another restaurant worker told the New York Post that the decision to remove the plaque had come from the diner’s “bosses.”

Denny’s reversed course well before Nvidia did. The chain says it learned of the removal on Friday, Nov. 13, and “put the plaque right…
items.t: ‘Some things you just don’t take off the menu’: Denny’s stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback

items.title: Sam Altman needs Jony Ive to create a physical AI device because Apple will never give OpenAI the real-world data ChatGPT needs, Tony Fadell says
items.summary:
Sam Altman asked former Apple design chief Jony Ive to create a physical device for OpenAI because the AI company cannot get the data it needs from the iPhones it runs on, Tony Fadell says. 

Fadell worked with Ive at Apple and is best known for being the “father of the iPod” and a co-creator of the iPhone. He founded Build Collective and previously founded Nest Labs. Fadell spoke to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon.

AI evidently works well for text, images, and video on the flat screens of our phones and laptops. So it is not obvious what an OpenAI consumer device would look like, or even do, given that ChatGPT can already function on any computing device you own. We know only that OpenAI hopes it will usurp the iPhone as the world’s most popular consumer electronics product.

The reason OpenAI is going to such lengths, Fadell believes, is because it needs data about the physical world that Apple refuses to give it due to privacy concerns.

“They have to build products because they cannot get contextual information out of the phone,” Fadell said. “So what they have to do is they have to recreate the GPS, the microphones, the speakers, the cameras, the temperature, you name it. Like, all kinds of different things that they have to get, because Apple will not allow you to get that out of the phone.”

“It’s really to get around all the restrictions because of all the privacy things for Apple. That’s why,” he said. “The more context that you have for AI, the better the answers, and the more quickly [you] can get to them.”

“Apple has all the products with all the context in…
items.t: Sam Altman needs Jony Ive to create a physical AI device because Apple will never give OpenAI the real-world data ChatGPT needs, Tony Fadell says

items.title: Thanksgiving as we know it was dreamed up by a women’s magazine editor who lobbied 5 presidents — Lincoln finally bit during the Civil War
items.summary:
It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.

Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys.

The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving ” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it.

Creating today’s Thanksgiving 

The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts . On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other.

The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book , which had the largest circulation of any…
items.t: Thanksgiving as we know it was dreamed up by a women’s magazine editor who lobbied 5 presidents — Lincoln finally bit during the Civil War

items.title: ‘Paid parental leave is no longer a nice-to-have’: New dads now take paid leave more often than new moms
items.summary:
You’re told to enjoy all the moments, good and bad, with your newborn because, sooner than later, you’ll blink and they’ll be adults shipping off to college and bringing back kids of their own. Unfortunately, feeding a growing baby now means trading those fleeting moments for labor hours, and rarely does a job’s parental leave policy include a special clause for “18 years of watching them grow up.”

Those lucky enough to have parents or other relatives who can look after their newborns can rely on them for a bit, while others who can afford it hire nannies and live-in help. The rest, reliant on dual-income households, opt to stagger their parental leave. Until recently, only the mom took time off from work.

For births before 1986, a first-time mother was more than three times as likely as a first-time father to take paid time off after the baby arrived. That gap has now flipped: from 2021 to 2025, 56.1% of first-time fathers took some form of paid leave in the 12 weeks after a birth, slightly more than the 52.5% of first-time mothers, according to a new KPMG Economics analysis of Census data . For births before 1986, just 11.5% of fathers took paid leave.

But now, counting unpaid time off, nearly three in four first-time fathers take leave after a birth, more than five times the 13.7% who did before 1986. The biggest jump came for births in the late 2010s, as states expanded paid leave programs and more employers began offering it as a benefit. For companies, the shift affects how they design leave policies, plan staffing and keep workers.

Paid vs. unpaid leave 

The…
items.t: ‘Paid parental leave is no longer a nice-to-have’: New dads now take paid leave more often than new moms

items.title: America’s missile stockpiles will take years to rebuild after Iran—and a watchdog warns the Pentagon has a blind spot
items.summary:
Over the past decade, the U.S. military bought an average of 86 Tomahawk cruise missiles a year. In the war with Iran, it has fired more than 1,000, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

That math explains why stockpiles of two of America’s most relied-upon weapons, the Tomahawk and the Patriot air-defense interceptor, will take years to refill. Under current Pentagon delivery projections, CSIS estimates the Tomahawks fired at Iran won’t be fully replaced until late 2030. The Army’s 3,203 Patriot interceptors requested for fiscal 2027 aren’t projected to start arriving until May 2029.

A new watchdog report says the Pentagon isn’t organized to close that gap. In “DOD Munitions: Planning and Leadership Needed to Address Persistent Shortages,” released Nov. 19, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the Defense Department has no overarching plan linking munitions production and funding to its requirements, and no office with the authority to carry one out. Fortune reported on the GAO’s findings this week.

Why Tomahawks and Patriots are so hard to replace 

Both weapons are Cold War designs. The National Air and Space Museum says Tomahawks were developed in the late 1970s and became fully operational in the early 1980s. The Patriot’s precursors date to the mid-1960s, and systems comparable to today’s arrived in the early 1980s, per CSIS.

The Tomahawk is a ship- and submarine-launched cruise missile with a range of roughly 1,000 miles. The Patriot is a defensive system that can intercept incoming missiles, drones, and manned…
items.t: America’s missile stockpiles will take years to rebuild after Iran—and a watchdog warns the Pentagon has a blind spot

items.title: Lori Huang’s Nvidia-funded foundation gained about $2.3 billion in a day on Jensen Huang’s return
items.summary:
When Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, shareholders weren’t the only winners. The Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, the private charity run by Huang’s wife, Lori, holds roughly 59 million Nvidia shares, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement.

Nvidia stock jumped more than 30% to close at $165.05, Fortune reported . At that price, the foundation’s stake was worth about $9.7 billion, roughly $2.3 billion more than it was worth at Friday’s close.

Huang told cheering employees at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters that he would be “a better CEO the second time around.” Wall Street seemed to agree: The S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025.

An 11-day round trip 

The rally erased much of the damage from Huang’s resignation, announced Nov. 12 . He stepped down after admitting to an affair and amid reports linking him to Alice Huang (no relation), a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials concluded was passing information to China, as well as a reported affair with a direct report. Chinese officials called the spying claims a fabrication.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 14.35% in intraday trading that day before closing down 4.34%.

A comeback campaign took shape almost immediately. An open letter started by an Nvidia employee had more than 206,000 names by Monday, including Elon Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. President Trump publicly urged the board to bring Huang back and called the board as it deliberated.

“There’s no one that can really replace…
items.t: Lori Huang’s Nvidia-funded foundation gained about $2.3 billion in a day on Jensen Huang’s return

items.title: ‘Look what I’ve produced’: Inside ‘peacock parenting,’ where kids become their parents’ status symbols
items.summary:
Today’s parents are consciously trying to break with how they were raised, prioritizing emotional well-being over punitive discipline. But a parenting phenomenon gaining attention seems at odds with that generational shift : “peacock parenting,” in which children become status symbols for their parents.

In ZERO TO THREE’s First Voice survey of more than 2,200 parents of children ages 5 and under, conducted this summer, 61% say they tell their kids “I love you” more often than their own parents did. Sixty percent say they focus more on their children’s mental health, and 56% say they won’t use the physical discipline they experienced growing up.

Peacock parenting describes a pattern of narcissistic behavior in which parents prioritize their own need for admiration and control over their children’s emotional needs. There’s no prevalence data specific to the term, and the underlying psychology is not new. What has changed is the public visibility of children’s lives, and the opportunities for parents to turn their kids’ achievements into social and financial capital.

Parenting has a new report card 

“Pride says, ‘I’m so happy for you.’ Peacocking says, ‘look what I’ve produced,’” says Dr. Christine Ghilain, a double board-certified clinical neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Health Neuropsychology in New Jersey. “It tips over when the moment is for the audience and not the child.”

She says the red flags include an achievement that doesn’t feel real until it’s been posted, moments staged or redone for the camera, repeated posting even after a child objects, and a…
items.t: ‘Look what I’ve produced’: Inside ‘peacock parenting,’ where kids become their parents’ status symbols

items.title: ‘Businesses hate chaos’: $166 billion in tariff refunds are flowing to companies, not the customers who paid
items.summary:
American companies are collecting roughly $166 billion in tariff refunds, plus interest, for costs that many consumers helped pay. Some of that money is going to bonuses.

At least nine public companies have disclosed using part of their refunds for executive or employee bonuses, according to a ProPublica investigation that used an AI tool to analyze securities filings and earnings calls. They include TJX , the owner of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls; Acushnet, which owns the golf brand Titleist; and the toolmaker Stanley Black & Decker.

TJX has set aside $167 million of its $463 million in refunds for incentive pay and discretionary bonuses for non-executive associates, according to its third-quarter earnings release , as Fortune reported last week . That is about 3% of the $5.5 billion TJX earned in its last fiscal year.

Acushnet disclosed that about $12 million of its $45.8 million in refunds would go to incentive compensation. Stanley Black & Decker, which is getting at least $298 million according to ProPublica’s refund database , hasn’t said how much will fund bonuses.

The money is landing with importers rather than the customers who absorbed higher prices, and few precedents exist for a scale like this.

“I think it’s fair to say that at this scale, it’s unprecedented, partly because the scale of business right now is unlike what we’ve seen in prior years,” Kathleen Claussen, a law professor at Georgetown University, told Fortune .

How emergency tariffs turned into a refund windfall 

In February 2025, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over illegal…
items.t: ‘Businesses hate chaos’: $166 billion in tariff refunds are flowing to companies, not the customers who paid

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its…
items.t: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar

items.title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
items.summary:
As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”

Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through cloud platform Vercel went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” 

Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

The case for ‘good enough’ AI 

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream…
items.t: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

items.title: They were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and in college when their friends got accused of cheating. Now their AI software polices 40 colleges
items.summary:
When OpenAI released ChatGPT on Nov. 30, 2022, Derin Suzener was a high school senior already leaning toward a career in AI. He got there “without having taken a single computer science course back in 11th grade,” he told Fortune . “I did not start using ChatGPT until I entered university, actually.”

Nikita Kravcenko, his future cofounder, was also in high school, taking AP classes where “my teachers were bombarding students with anti-AI policy, because it was like a new technology at that point,” he said. “So they were very fearful of what it could do and write. So they were essentially having a craze over it.”

By the time they got to Purdue, the craze had casualties. “I was seeing all of my friends get accused of cheating with AI on their computer science assignments,” Suzener said. “And they would have a pretty hard time proving it, actually.”

So Suzener, Kravcenko and two classmates built a way to prove it. Their company, Remora, makes Syntax, a document editor that records how a student writes a paper (typing speed, cursor movement, what gets pasted in) and flags anything odd for the teacher to review. The founders say it’s used in classrooms at 40 U.S. colleges and universities, though they declined to name any, saying that identifying customers could help larger competitors go after the same schools. The company says four more institutions will start using it next semester. Students can also buy it themselves, starting at $9.99 for three months.

The pitch is protection for students who did their own work. “The guilty are truly proven to be guilty, and then the…
items.t: They were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and in college when their friends got accused of cheating. Now their AI software polices 40 colleges

items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

items.title: Democrats must unite on AI regulation. Here’s our three-point plan | Nathan E Sanders and Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Voters are demanding action on the issue. We need to make AI work for the American public, not the tech oligarchs

This month’s elections demonstrated the American public’s urgent demand for change. But they also revealed a glaring problem for the Democrats’ policy agenda: they haven’t presented a compelling plan around AI.

This is important, because AI isn’t just a political issue in itself: it’s also a primary force behind both the economic disruption and political corruption that drove so many voters to the polls.

items.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
items.summary:
It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now

The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times.

When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP.

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and…
items.t: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
